commentary: Aquinas reads this chapter as a set of preparatory doubts that the science of wisdom must clear away about itself before it can proceed to its proper subject, separate substance. He organizes the puzzles under three headings. First, is wisdom a single science, given that it studies several first principles which, unlike the objects of other sciences, are not themselves contraries? Aquinas answers that wisdom remains one science because its many principles are all reducible to a single genus, namely being; this is the same reasoning by which a science of contraries counts as one, since contraries too share a genus. Second, does wisdom examine the common principles used in demonstration, such as 'the whole is greater than its part'? Aquinas says yes, and principally so, because it is wisdom's business to know the common notions - being, non-being, whole, part - that underlie such principles, and the particular sciences merely borrow this knowledge from it. Third, does wisdom study all substances, and does it treat accidents as well as substances? Aquinas holds that it studies all substances insofar as they share the one genus of being-through-itself, though separate, immaterial substances receive its principal attention, and it treats accidents only in reference to the substances of which they are demonstrated. He also addresses whether wisdom concerns the four causes treated in physics, denying that mathematical objects or Platonic Forms exist as separate entities, and closes by weighing whether genera or species better deserve the name of principle - concluding that genera, being simpler and containing many species potentially, have the better claim, even though species are in another sense more indivisible.

Continuing the survey of unresolved doubts, Aquinas here treats questions about what wisdom's subject-matter actually consists in. He first asks whether anything exists beyond singular sensible things for this science to consider, since a science of pure individuals is impossible - individuals being infinite in number and therefore unknowable scientifically. His resolution is characteristically careful: nothing exists in reality apart from singulars themselves, but the intellect can and does abstract common natures from them, and it is these universal natures, not free-standing entities, that intelligible science grasps. He then asks the more pressing question whether any substance actually separate from sensible things exists. Aquinas affirms that such substances do exist, but he is emphatic that they are not the separated Forms or Ideas of sensible kinds that Plato imagined; rather, as he will show later in the work, they are the first unmoved movers, and only these deserve the name. He works through the further puzzle of whether matter or form has the better claim to be a first principle, concluding that since matter is only ever in potency while form is actuality, form is by nature prior - yet sensible forms are themselves corruptible, so an eternal separate substance is still needed to explain why the world exhibits lasting order at all. Aquinas also rejects the idea that unity and being function as genera, since no differentia can be said to 'participate' in them, and dismisses attempts to make points, lines, or numerical units into self-subsisting principles, since these are merely divisions or limits of continuous magnitudes and cannot exist apart from what they limit.

Here Aquinas explains how a single science can study something said in many senses. He notes that if 'being' were purely equivocal, with nothing shared across its uses, no one science could investigate it, since a science requires a genuine common subject. But being is not spoken of that way; it resembles terms like 'medical' or 'healthy', which are used of many different things - an instrument, a diet, a complexion - not because they share one definition, but because each is related in its own way back to a single reference point, namely medicine or health. Aquinas calls this kind of unity analogical, standing midway between strict univocity, where a term means exactly the same thing in every application, and sheer equivocity, where it means something wholly different each time. Being works analogically in just this fashion: substance is called being in the primary sense, because it has existence properly in itself, while quality, quantity, and the other categories are called beings only because they are dispositions or determinations of substance. Because everything reduces to this one focal meaning, and because every real contrariety likewise reduces to a first contrariety within being, philosophy - unlike physics, which studies things as movable, or dialectic and sophistic, which trade in the same terms without penetrating to being as such - can treat all beings as belonging to one science. Aquinas also clarifies an apparent problem about privative opposites that admit an intermediate, such as just and unjust: the privation here removes only the complete, perfect degree of the positive term, not its entire meaning, which is why partial failures in obedience to law can occupy a middle ground.

Aquinas shows here how first philosophy relates to mathematics and physics by comparing how each uses the common axioms of demonstration, such as the principle that equals taken from equals leave equals. The mathematician relies on this axiom constantly but only within his own restricted domain, applying it to lines, numbers, or angles considered strictly as continuous quantities, without regard to whether these quantities exist as beings in the fuller sense. It belongs to first philosophy, by contrast, to consider such common axioms in their full universality, as they hold of anything whatsoever insofar as it is a being, not merely insofar as it is quantified. Aquinas draws the same comparison with natural science: physics studies the principles and properties of the things that are, but only insofar as they are subject to motion, whereas the primary science studies the same underlying subjects insofar as they simply exist, prescinding from the character of being movable. Because of this difference in the formal object under which each science considers its material, both mathematics and physics turn out to be, in a sense, particular or partial sciences falling under the single universal science of wisdom, which alone examines being as being and therefore alone can adjudicate on the principles that every subordinate science silently presupposes. This is why, Aquinas notes, it belongs properly to the philosopher rather than to the mathematician to investigate the ultimate justification of these common axioms.

Aquinas here treats the principle that the same thing cannot both be and not be in the same respect at the same time, which he identifies as the first and most certain of all principles precisely because its terms, being and non-being, are the first things grasped by the intellect. Because nothing is more basic from which it could be derived, this principle cannot be demonstrated in the strict sense; it can only be defended 'ad hominem', by compelling an opponent who denies it into self-contradiction. Aquinas lays out three lines of argument used for this purpose. First, meaningful speech requires that a word signify one determinate thing; anyone who says 'this is and is not' has, by uttering the negation, unsaid what his own affirmation just signified, which destroys the possibility of communication itself. Second, if a statement is true it signifies something with a certain necessity, and what is necessarily so cannot simultaneously fail to be so; hence contradictory statements about the same subject cannot both be true. Third, if affirmation and its contradictory negation were equally true, no statement would be any more accurate than its opposite, collapsing all distinctions - one could then say with equal justice that a man is a horse. Aquinas notes that these arguments are aimed specifically at Heraclitus, who held that opposites can be simultaneously true of the same thing, and observes that Heraclitus adopted this position without grasping its full consequences, since even the claim that opposites can both be true would, by its own logic, be no truer than its denial, destroying rational discourse altogether.

Aquinas turns next to Protagoras's dictum that man is the measure of all things, which he treats as a variant of the error just rebutted, since it implies that whatever appears to someone is true for that person, so that contradictory judgments about the same thing could both stand. He traces this opinion to two sources: the natural philosophers' assumption that nothing can come to be from what simply is not, which seemed to force one to say a thing must already be both white and not-white before it changes; and the observation that different people judge the same things differently, as tastes seem pleasant to some and unpleasant to others. Aquinas resolves the first difficulty by recalling the distinction between existing potentially and existing actually - what becomes white comes from what is only potentially white, not from sheer non-being. Against the second, he insists it is childish to weigh every appearance as equally authoritative, since the same object never seems sweet to one and bitter to another unless a sense organ has been damaged; the untainted judgment is the true measure. He adds further considerations: the heavenly bodies remain constant and provide a fixed standard for truth; motion presupposes something moved from a determinate start to a determinate end, impossible if contradictories held simultaneously; medical and dietary practice assumes real, stable natures in things; and if only human perception seems unstable, this reflects our own condition, not flux in the world. Aquinas concludes that neither Heraclitus nor Anaxagoras, who held everything is present actually in everything, can be right, since both views make contraries predicable of the same subject at once.

Aquinas compares wisdom to the other theoretical sciences along three lines. First, regarding how each science obtains its basic definitions: every particular science assumes rather than demonstrates the essence of its subject, arriving at it either through sense observation or by borrowing it from a higher science. Natural philosophy studies mobile things whose definitions include sensible matter; mathematics studies things that, while existing in sensible matter, can be defined without reference to it, since their properties do not depend on matter being of any particular sensible kind; wisdom alone studies substances that are wholly separate from matter and immobile. Second, among the theoretical sciences - physics, mathematics, and what Aquinas calls theology or divine science - theology ranks highest in nobility, because a science's dignity follows the dignity of its object, and the separate, immaterial substances that theology studies are the most excellent of existing things. Third, Aquinas explains why wisdom alone, among the theoretical sciences, can be called universal: physics and mathematics each mark off one determinate class of being for themselves, whereas wisdom considers being qua being and the first principles from which every particular being and its own principles ultimately derive, making it prior to and more comprehensive than the others. He also revisits the classic example distinguishing 'snub', whose definition necessarily includes matter (a snub nose), from 'concave', whose definition does not, applying this distinction to show that the natural philosopher must define things like flesh or the eye with reference to their matter, while wisdom's separate substances require no such reference at all.

Aquinas explains here why there can be no science of accidental being, that is, of what happens neither always, nor for the most part, nor by any determinate necessity, but merely by chance. No recognized art or science concerns itself with such accidents: architecture does not consider whether the inhabitants of a house will be happy there, and no craft studies what merely happens to coincide in a subject without following from its essential nature. Only sophistic exploits this kind of accidental predication, which is why, Aquinas notes, Plato was right to say the sophist trades in a kind of non-being. Aquinas gives the reason no science can grasp such things: every science concerns what is invariable or at least regular, but the accidental by definition escapes both categories, arising from no determinate or ordered cause. He adds an important argument: if accidental events had determinate causes in the way essential effects do, then tracing any causal chain back far enough would show that everything happens of necessity, eliminating chance and contingency from the world altogether - an unacceptable conclusion. Aquinas then distinguishes accidental being from two other extended senses of 'being': being as truth or falsity, which is merely a construction of the mind in judging by combining or dividing concepts, and therefore not something wisdom investigates as a reality outside the mind; and being by chance or fortune, which he defines as an accidental cause operating within events that are ordered toward an end by nature or by deliberate purpose. Because fortune presupposes purposeful or natural causation and is not itself a per se cause of anything, Aquinas concludes that accidental causes, including fortune, are always posterior to and dependent upon essential causes such as reason and nature.

Aquinas here works through Aristotle's definition of motion, one of the more difficult notions in philosophy. He sets out several premises: being divides into potency and actuality; being divides into the ten categories; motion does not constitute some further, eleventh category, but tracks the same division of potency and act found within each category; and within any genus - substance, quality, quantity, place - one finds both a complete, perfected state and an incomplete, imperfect one. On this basis Aquinas explains motion as the actuality of what exists potentially, precisely insofar as it is still potential - neither the bare potency itself, since the potential as such need not be undergoing anything, nor the fully realized actuality that terminates the process, since once the house exists building has ceased, but the incomplete actuality lying between the two, occurring exactly while the potential is being brought toward its term. He illustrates this with bronze, which is potentially a statue: the actuality of the bronze precisely as bronze is not motion, but its actuality precisely as buildable-toward-something-else is. This is why motion is so hard to classify, and why others mistakenly called it a kind of otherness, inequality, or indeterminacy: it is neither pure potency nor complete actuality, but a real hybrid of the two. Finally, motion resides properly in the thing moved rather than in the mover, since the actuality of the power to move and the actuality of what is moved are, in underlying reality, one and the same process, differing only in the respect under which each is considered - much as the road from Thebes to Athens and from Athens to Thebes is a single road under two descriptions.

Turning to the infinite, a property attaching to motion and to quantity generally, Aquinas first distinguishes four senses of the untraversable or infinite: what is by its very kind incapable of being traversed at all, as a point cannot, in the way a sound cannot be seen; what has only begun to be traversed and not yet completed; what could in principle be traversed but so vastly exceeds any traverser's actual power that it is infinite for practical purposes, like the depth of the sea; and what is naturally suited to have a limit but simply lacks one, which alone is the infinite in the strict sense. He also distinguishes infinity by addition, as with number, to which a unit can always be added, from infinity by division, as with continuous magnitude, always further divisible, noting time and motion are infinite both ways at once. Aquinas then reports and endorses arguments that no actually infinite substance can exist, separate as the Platonists supposed or inhering in a sensible body as the early naturalists held: an infinite substance, having no quantity or plurality of its own, would have to be indivisible, yet the genuinely infinite must be quantified, a contradiction; and if divisible, every part of it would itself have to be infinite, impossible since a whole is always greater than its part. He further rehearses the naturalistic arguments against any actually infinite sensible body, composite (since its elements are finite in number and must remain proportionate to preserve the mixture) or simple (since each element has a determinate active power, and an infinite element would overpower and destroy the others), concluding that no sensible or intelligible body, and no separately existing number, can actually be infinite.

Aquinas here classifies the different ways something can be said to change. Change occurs accidentally when something changes only because something associated with it changes, as when 'the musician walks' or a sailor is said to move because his ship moves; it occurs per se but only partially when a part of a thing changes, as a body is healed because its eye is healed; and it occurs per se and primarily when the whole subject itself is directly moved, as when a stone falls. Aquinas draws the identical threefold distinction on the side of the mover. He then identifies five elements present in every change - the primary mover, the thing moved, the time of the change, and the two termini, that from which and that to which it proceeds - observing that change is properly differentiated by these termini rather than by mover, subject, or time, which are common to every change. Working through the possible combinations of positive and negative termini, Aquinas shows that change from a negative state to nothing in particular is no real change, leaving three genuine types: change from a negative term to its positive contradictory, which is generation; change from a positive term to its negative contradictory, which is destruction; and change between two positive contrary or intermediate terms, which alone deserves the name motion in the strict sense. He explains why generation and destruction are not themselves motion: since non-being cannot properly be said to be moved, and what comes to be is, in the relevant respect, not yet in being, generation cannot be classified as a movement, though it remains a real kind of change alongside motion proper.

Aquinas here explains why motion in the strict sense can occur only in three categories - quality, quantity, and place. Since motion always runs between contraries or their intermediates, and only these three categories admit true contrariety of a determinate, continuous kind, there can be no motion in substance (only generation and corruption, whose termini are contradictories, not contraries), in relation (change occurs there only accidentally, when a correlative shifts because its partner changes), or in action and passion. Aquinas addresses the seeming counterexample of fire and water, which appear contrary as substances; he rejects treating heat and cold as themselves the substantial forms of these elements, and rejects letting substantial forms admit degrees like accidents, concluding they are contrary only in the qualified sense that one implies the intelligible privation of another, as animate opposes inanimate. He then gives several arguments against 'motion of motion' or 'becoming of becoming', among them that this would make motion its own subject of further change, and that it would generate an infinite regress with no first term, leaving nothing able to come to be at all. Aquinas closes by distinguishing three senses of 'immobile' - what cannot possibly be moved, as God; what could be moved only with great difficulty; and what is naturally movable but simply is not moving under its proper conditions, which alone is properly called rest, since rest is the privation of motion in a subject capable of motion. He then defines the spatial relations structuring local motion - together, apart, contact, betweenness, contrariety of place, succession, contiguity, continuity - closing by distinguishing the point from the numerical unit, since points admit contact and always have something between any two, while units, related only by succession, do not.
